items.title: The Second Dhyāna: Inner Clarity Replacing Applied and Sustained Thought

items.zh: 於有尋有伺三摩地相，心能棄捨。於無尋無伺三摩地相，繫念安住。於諸怱務所行境界能正遠離，於不怱務所行境界安住其心；一味寂靜、極寂靜轉，是故說言：尋伺寂靜故、內等淨故。
items.en: The mind becomes able to relinquish the mark of concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and fixes its mindfulness instead, abiding, on the mark of concentration free of both … it correctly withdraws from every object involving hurried activity, and settles the mind instead in an object free of such hurried activity, turning uniformly still, utterly still. For this reason it is said: because applied and sustained thought have become still, and because of inner, uniform purity.

items.zh: 又彼即於無尋無伺三摩地中串修習故，超過尋伺有間缺位，能正獲得無間缺位，是故說言：心一趣故。無尋無伺者，一切尋伺悉皆斷故。
items.en: And by repeatedly cultivating this concentration free of applied and sustained thought, one passes beyond the stage where such thought still intermittently intrudes, and genuinely attains the stage where it no longer intrudes at all — for this reason it is said: because the mind reaches a single direction. Free of applied and sustained thought means that all applied and sustained thought has been entirely cut off.

items.zh: 所言定者，謂已獲得加行究竟作意故。所言生者，由此為因、由此為緣，無間所生，故名定生。言喜樂者，謂已獲得所希求義，又於喜中未見過失，有欣有喜；一切尋伺初靜慮地諸煩惱品所有麁重皆遠離故，能對治彼廣大輕安身心調柔有堪能樂所隨逐故，名有喜樂。依順次數，此為第二。如是一切，如前應知。復次，

items.title: The Third Dhyāna: Equanimity Arrives, and Why Only Now

items.zh: 彼於喜相深見過失，是故說言：於喜離欲。又於爾時，遠離二種亂心災患，能於離喜第三靜慮攝持其心。第二靜慮已離尋伺，今於此中復離於喜，是故說言：安住於捨。如是二法能擾亂心，障無間捨。初靜慮中有尋伺故，令無間捨不自在轉；第二靜慮由有喜故，令無間捨不自在轉。是故此捨，初二靜慮說名無有。由是因緣，修靜慮者，第三靜慮方名有捨。由有
items.en: One sees deeply into the fault of the mark of joy, and for this reason it is said: one becomes free of desire for joy itself … these two things — applied-and-sustained-thought and joy — are each able to disturb the mind, obstructing uninterrupted equanimity. In the first dhyāna, because applied and sustained thought remain, uninterrupted equanimity cannot yet operate freely; in the second dhyāna, because joy remains, uninterrupted equanimity likewise cannot yet operate freely. For this reason this equanimity is said to be absent in the first and second dhyānas. On account of these causes and conditions, it is only in the third dhyāna that one cultivating dhyāna is said to possess equanimity.

items.zh: 捨故，如如安住所有正念，如是如是彼喜俱行想及作意不復現行。若復於此第三靜慮不善修故，或時失念，彼喜俱行想及作意時復現行，尋即速疾以慧通達，能正了知，隨所生起能不忍受，方便棄捨、除遣、變吐，心住上捨，是故說有正念、正知。彼於爾時，住如是捨、正念、正知，親近、修習、多修習故，令心踊躍俱行喜受便得除滅。離喜寂靜、最極寂靜，與喜相違心受生起。彼於爾時，色身、意身領納受樂及輕安樂，是故說言：有身受樂。第三靜慮已下諸地，無如是樂及無間捨；第三靜慮已上諸地，此無間捨雖復可得，而無有樂。下地樂捨俱無有故，上地有捨而無樂故，是故說言：於是處所，謂第三靜慮，諸聖宣說。謂依於此已得安住補特伽羅，具足捨、念及以正知，住身受樂，第三靜慮具足安住。言諸聖者，謂佛世尊及佛弟子。復次，此中對治種類勢相似故，略不宣說樂斷對治，但說對治所作樂斷。何等名為此中對治？所謂捨、念、及以正知。由即於此數修習故，便能棄捨令不出離第三靜慮第三靜慮地中勝樂，是故
items.en: Commentary — Question: mindfulness, clear comprehension, and equanimity are present everywhere; why are they left unmentioned at the first dhyāna and so on? Answer: in the first dhyāna, since it is brought about through the gateway of applied and sustained thought, though present, they go unmentioned. In the second dhyāna, since there is still joy's own exuberant activity and a slight remaining affliction still enveloping the mind, the whole is instead named simply by "inner purity." In the third dhyāna, since even that slight remaining affliction is entirely gone, its own distinct character can finally be shown.

items.title: The Fourth Dhyāna: Happiness Itself Abandoned, Every Storm Stilled

items.zh: 修靜慮者，即於爾時，所有苦樂皆得超越。由是因緣，若先所斷、若今所斷，總集說言：樂斷、苦斷，先喜憂沒。謂入第四靜慮定時，樂受斷故；入第二靜慮定時，苦受斷故；入第三靜慮定時，喜受沒故；入初靜慮定時，憂受沒故。
items.en: One cultivating dhyāna, at that very time, transcends whatever suffering and happiness remain … that is: on entering the fourth dhyāna, the feeling of happiness is cut off; on entering the second dhyāna, the feeling of suffering is cut off; on entering the third dhyāna, the feeling of joy vanishes; on entering the first dhyāna, the feeling of grief vanishes.

items.zh: 今於此中，且約苦、樂二受斷故，說有所餘非苦樂受，是故說言：彼於爾時不苦不樂。
從初靜慮一切下地災患已斷。謂尋、伺、喜樂、入息、出息。由彼斷故，此中捨念清淨鮮白。由是因緣，正入第四靜慮定時，心住無動，一切動亂皆悉遠離，是故說言：捨念清淨。
items.en: Every disturbance of the lower stages, from the first dhyāna onward, is now cut off — namely, applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, in-breath, and out-breath. Because these are cut off, equanimity and mindfulness here become pure and bright … at the very moment of entering the fourth dhyāna, the mind abides utterly unmoved, every disturbance entirely left behind — for this reason it is said: purified equanimity, purified mindfulness.

items.zh: 第四等言，如前所說初靜慮等，應知其相。復次，

blocks.text: The classical descriptions of the higher absorptions, each explained. Two short passages are untranslated.

"The mind relinquishes the mark of concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and fixes mindfulness on concentration free of both." "Turning uniformly still": **inner clarity** and **one-pointedness**, with "joy and happiness born of concentration". Venerable Miào Jìng: how still? "You don't even hear thunder in the sky."

"One sees deeply into the fault of joy", and becomes "free of desire for joy itself". Applied thought and joy "each disturb the mind, obstructing uninterrupted equanimity". Only now is one said to have **equanimity**, **mindfulness**, and **clear comprehension**, and to "experience happiness with the body". Why are these not mentioned earlier? Because in the first and second absorptions, though present, they are overshadowed by thought and joy.

"On entering the fourth absorption, happiness is cut off; on entering the second, suffering; on entering the third, joy." Venerable Miào Jìng: each feeling is cut at its own stage, in sequence, not all at once. "Every disturbance of the lower stages (applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, in-breath, out-breath) is now cut off." "Equanimity and mindfulness become pure and bright." Venerable Miào Jìng: up to the third absorption one breathes; in the fourth, breathing stops.

The absorptions are not described as mystical states but as a sequence of simplifications: thought goes, then joy, then happiness, then even the breath. Each step is driven by seeing the fault in what remains.

quiz.q: In the second dhyāna "the mind relinquishes concentration with thought." What does Venerable Miào Jìng say the first dhyāna's thought becomes?
options: moving to the second, the first's thought becomes defiling
quiz.why: "The mind becomes able to relinquish the mark of concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought." Venerable Miào Jìng: going from the first to the second dhyāna, which surpasses the first, the first's thought is a defiling factor — it becomes defilement. (Earlier, from access to the first, thought was pure, abandoning desire.)

quiz.q: "Free of thought means all thought is cut off" — the English adds "directed towards desire." What does Venerable Miào Jìng say?
options: not without discrimination — just not the first dhyāna's or desire realm's kind of thought
quiz.why: "Free of applied and sustained thought means that all applied and sustained thought directed towards desire has been entirely cut off." Venerable Miào Jìng: being free of thought doesn't mean there's no discrimination; there is, but not the kind of thought found in the first dhyāna or desire realm. "Directed towards desire" isn't in the original.

quiz.q: "Only in the third dhyāna is one said to have equanimity." What does Venerable Miào Jìng say of the first and second?
options: only at the third — not yet at the first and second
quiz.why: "On account of these causes, it is only in the third dhyāna that one cultivating dhyāna is said to possess equanimity." Venerable Miào Jìng: only at the third dhyāna is it called "having equanimity"; the first and second can't yet be said to have it.

quiz.q: "These two things disturb the mind, obstructing uninterrupted equanimity." How do the masters read "two things"?
options: Miào Jìng: thought is one, joy the other; Cháng Bǎi, via Miào Jìng, links inner faults to the three calamities — thought to fire, joy to water, bliss and breath to wind
quiz.why: "These two things are each able to disturb the mind, obstructing uninterrupted equanimity." Venerable Miào Jìng: thought is one, joy is the other — that reading also works. Master Cháng Bǎi: the first dhyāna's thought brings the outer calamity of fire, the second's joy brings water, the third's bliss and breathing bring wind.

quiz.q: Pleasure, pain, joy, and grief each cease at different dhyānas. Do they cease together, according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: not together — each at its stage, in sequence
quiz.why: "On entering the fourth dhyāna, the feeling of happiness is cut off; on entering the second dhyāna, the feeling of suffering is cut off." Venerable Miào Jìng: removing these feelings is assigned to stages — each cut at its stage, not simultaneously, in sequence.

quiz.q: The fourth dhyāna cuts "thought, joy, bliss, in-breath, out-breath." Where does Venerable Miào Jìng say breathing stops?
options: present through the third, gone at the fourth
quiz.why: "Namely, applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, in-breath, and out-breath." Venerable Miào Jìng: those up to the third dhyāna all breathe; at the fourth dhyāna, breathing stops.
